Navigating stormy waters: reflections on monetary policy
summary_150w:
Frankfurt am Main, 5 November 2026
The past seven years have been an extraordinary journey. [ 1 ]
We have moved from a world in which inflation was persistently too low to one marked by recurrent inflationary shocks; from a historically accommodative monetary policy stance to the fastest tightening cycle in the history of the ECB; and from a deeply integrated global economy to one increasingly shaped by fragmentation and geopolitical tensions. As I reach the end of my journey here at the ECB, I would like to reflect on the lessons these experiences have taught me about the conduct of monetary policy in a world that has become less predictable. My remarks today are personal reflections on how the experience of recent years has shaped my thinking about monetary policy and what it may teach us about navigating the challenges ahead. There are four key takeaways. The first takeaway is that central banks should prioritise instruments that allow them to adjust monetary policy quickly as conditions change. We entered the pandemic after a long period in which inflation had been below our target (Slide 2, left-hand side). Globalisation, and the integration of China in particular, had structurally lowered the global cost of producing goods, putting downward pressure on inflation. At the same time, the global financial crisis and the sovereign debt crisis had weakened public and private balance sheets and left lasting scars on demand, weighing on economic activity and inflation. Over time, this experience gradually fostered the belief that these forces were permanent, leaving monetary policy primarily focused on bringing inflation back up to target. As a result, after chronically overpredicting inflation before the pandemic, we were slow to recognise that we had entered a new regime in which we would repeatedly underpredict it (Slide 2, right-hand side). Indeed, even as evidence of a more substantial and persistent rise in inflation was mounting, the initial reaction was one of relief: the economy finally seemed to be escaping the low-inflation environment. [ 2 ]
But the rapid increase in the share of goods and services experiencing inflation above 2% signalled that price pressures were becoming increasingly broad-based (Slide 3). This exposed two key features of the inflation process that our analytical frameworks had not sufficiently accounted for. One was the steepening of the Phillips curve, which was in part a result of more frequent price changes as firms sought to protect their profit margins in the face of sharp cost increases (Slide 4). The other, related feature was the role of firms’ profits in inflation. Unlike the high-inflation period of the 1970s, when inflation was almost entirely driven by growth in unit labour costs, the post-pandemic inflation surge was to a significant extent driven by rising unit profits (Slide 5). [ 3 ]
So, the pandemic was a structural break in many of the trends we had witnessed before. This included a shift in the global balance between savings and investment.

title: Shaping the future of money
summary_150w:
Tirana, 5 November 2026
Money connects people and societies. But to do this, it must be trusted. It must allow people and businesses to transact safely and efficiently. And it must evolve with geopolitical and technological developments. For centuries, central banks have issued money and safeguarded its value. That mandate remains unchanged. But the environment in which money is used is being transformed. People are increasingly paying digitally. Tokenisation could reorganise the financial value chain. New solutions are being considered to enhance cross-border payments. And geopolitical fragmentation is making the resilience and governance of critical infrastructure ever more important. Central banks must therefore ensure that the money they issue remains fit for the future. This does not mean replacing the private sector or predicting which technology will prevail. It means providing a trusted public foundation for payments and finance on which private innovation can flourish. And it means preventing digitalisation from increasing fragmentation or creating new dependencies. This is why the Eurosystem has adopted a comprehensive payments strategy. [ 1 ]
The strategy has four objectives: ensuring that central bank money can continue to settle retail and wholesale transactions as preferences and technologies evolve; strengthening Europe’s resilience and strategic autonomy; fostering an integrated, competitive and innovative payments ecosystem; and supporting the international role of the euro. In other words, we are seeking to comprehensively upgrade money and payments in Europe. The Western Balkans are also taking active policy steps to enhance and integrate payments in the region. Several countries, including Albania, have already joined the Single Euro Payments Area. And a clone of the Eurosystem’s fast payment system (TIPS), developed by Banca d’Italia, is already fully operational in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Montenegro and will soon be launched in Albania, Kosovo and North Macedonia. It allows real-time, low-cost domestic transactions in local currencies around the clock, every day of the year. This represents real, tangible progress that people will benefit from in their daily lives. But we must always think one step ahead. So today, I will discuss four key initiatives we are working on. We are modernising euro banknotes. We are developing a digital euro. We are making it possible to settle tokenised asset transactions in central bank money and creating the conditions for an integrated and innovative tokenised finance ecosystem. And we are interlinking fast payment systems to make cross-border payments faster and more efficient. These initiatives have a common goal: ensuring access to safe public money while creating space for private innovation and international cooperation. Let me begin with the most familiar form of central bank money: cash. In discussions about digitalisation, cash is sometimes talked about as a technology of the past. That is a mistake. In an age where cyber risks, hybrid threats and system outages make the headlines, cash remains the most resilient form of payment we have. More than 31 billion euro banknotes, worth over €1.6 trillion, are in circulation. People do not just see cash as a means of payment; they also view it as a store of value and a safeguard in periods of uncertainty.

title: The EBA publishes revised Guidelines on internal governance, delivering greater proportionality and simplification for banks
summary_150w:
The European Banking Authority (EBA) today published its revised Guidelines on internal governance under the Capital Requirements Directive (CRD). The revised Guidelines reflect the changes introduced by CRD VI and form part of the EBA’s broader commitment to simplify the regulatory framework, strengthen proportionality and reduce unnecessary compliance burdens, while safeguarding sound and robust governance across the EU banking sector. The revision follows the entry into force of Directive (EU) 2024/1619 (CRD VI), which amends Directive 2013/36/EU. CRD VI strengthens certain governance requirements, including the introduction a mapping of duties and responsibilities for members of the management body and key function holders, as well as a dedicated  governance framework for third-country branches. The revised Guidelines provide further clarity on internal governance arrangements, including the responsibilities of the management body, organisational structures, management of conflict of interest including in relation to the combination of Chair and executive functions, and key aspects of internal control frameworks. They also introduce a more proportionate and risk-based approach to governance requirements ensuring that expectations remain aligned with institutions' size, nature and complexity. The final Guidelines take into account feedback received from stakeholders during the public consultation and targeted outreach activities. By focusing on the elements that are most relevant for effective sound governance, the revised Guidelines maintain strong governance provisions while reducing unnecessary operational and compliance burdens for institutions. The Guidelines have been developed pursuant to Article 74 of Directive 2013/36/EU which mandates the EBA to further harmonise institutions' governance arrangements, processes and mechanisms across the European Union.       Norway and Switzerland. It was established in 1960 by the EFTA Convention ​ ​ (revised in 2001) to promote free trade and economic integration between its members,
      within Europe, and globally. Three EFTA States (Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway)
      together with the EU Member States are part of the European Economic Area (EEA), established by the EEA Agreement (see a summary of the EEA Agreement ). This agreement entered into force in 1994. Its objective is to extend the EU’s
      Internal Market to the three EFTA States that are part of the EEA. It guarantees equal
      rights and obligations within the Internal Market for individuals and economic operators
      in the EEA. All relevant Internal Market legislation is integrated into the EEA Agreement so that
      it applies throughout the whole of the EEA. The core of these rules relates to the
      free movement of goods, capital, services and persons. In addition, the EEA Agreement
      covers ‘horizontal’ areas such as social policy, consumer protection, environment,
      company law, statistics, tourism and culture. To ensure equal conditions of competition
      throughout the EEA, the EEA Agreement mirrors the competition and state aid rules
      of the EU Treaties . It also provides for participation in the EU programmes such as those for research
